messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Since the hurricane that struck the Gulf Coast three years ago, Tane’s life had narrowed in ways that made sense to him but left him feeling increasingly cut off. He was a 46-year-old auditor, a widower who had built his days around order, schedules, and careful review, and on the night of the storm that order vanished. He had been in a hotel for work, several floors up, when the power failed and the building went black. The wind screamed through broken seals, alarms cut in and out, and the stairwell filled with a damp, chemical smell from floodwater and generator fumes. He remembered gripping the rail in the dark, mouth full of a metallic, dirty taste, waiting for updates that never came, convinced each delay meant the building was giving way and there was nothing he could do to stop it.

In the months afterward, the parts of ordinary life that should have felt good or neutral began to unsettle him most. If he caught himself relaxing at home after dinner, or felt unexpectedly happy during a quiet evening, he would tense almost immediately, as if calm were the moment danger slipped in unnoticed. Nighttime was especially difficult. Waking in darkness brought back the sense of being trapped in that powerless hotel, and certain physical locations—parking garages, stairwells, older office buildings, unfamiliar client sites—could make his body react before he had time to think. When that happened he would light a cigarette, step outside, keep moving, and avoid settling long enough to feel anything; he had also stopped talking with other people about the hurricane or what followed, because even brief conversation about it seemed to pull him too close to something he could not control.

The triggers also sharpened his sense that threat was always close. Silence in a building, especially after business hours, no longer felt peaceful to Tane; unusual quiet made him brace, listening for what was about to go wrong. If an elevator stalled for a moment, if a report upload took too long, if a colleague was late answering a message, his mind leapt to catastrophe. At client visits he often stayed near exits and resisted going into parts of a building he did not know well, telling himself he needed to assess the danger first. The same moments could bring back the disaster with disturbing sensory force. In the dark, or when he entered certain locations, he could suddenly smell the rank mix of floodwater and fuel again and taste the foul metallicness that had filled his mouth that night; at times the memory was so extreme it felt unreal, as if he were describing something that had happened to someone else.

What had settled most deeply was his conviction that the world was dangerous and that he was fundamentally helpless inside it. He had come to believe that bad things happened without warning and that no amount of preparation could truly stop them. That belief made him scan harder in silence and grow more alarmed by delays, because any pause seemed like proof that disaster was already unfolding somewhere out of sight. It also colored the way he remembered the hurricane: the sensory fragments arrived with more force when he was caught in that helpless frame of mind, and the very extremity of the memory reinforced his feeling that normal rules did not apply and safety could not be trusted.

Over time his ways of coping deepened the problem. He smoked more heavily during the workday, especially before entering unfamiliar office buildings, and structured his schedule to avoid lingering anywhere that might let him relax. As an auditor, he used to be known for his ease on site, but now he rushed inspections, asked to switch assignments, and avoided small talk with clients if it drifted toward weather, emergencies, or personal life. Refusing to talk and never letting himself settle brought a temporary sense of control, yet afterward he felt more dead inside, more convinced something essential in him had shut down. That numbness seemed to confirm his bleak view of himself and the world, and it left him even less willing to risk ease, pleasure, or openness with other people.

The pattern had tightened further in the past year. Because he spent so much effort staying guarded, even moments of happiness had started to feel like triggers in their own right, almost a warning sign that he was about to be blindsided. The more he avoided relaxing and kept to known places, the more foreign and dangerous unfamiliar settings became. The more he scanned for danger, the more easily sensory fragments of the hurricane broke through; and once those smells and tastes returned, he became certain he was right not to trust silence, darkness, or delay.

Tane sought help only after he nearly walked out of an overnight audit at a downtown hotel when a brief power fluctuation dimmed the hallway lights. Standing there with a cigarette in his shaking hand, tasting that old metallic bitterness, he was struck by how small his life had become. What frightened him most was not just another memory, but the sense that he would remain trapped in vigilance and emptiness, unable to feel safe even in the rare moments that should have brought relief. What he hopes for, though he says it cautiously, is to stop living as if the storm is still deciding what to take from him.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that triggers themselves lead to or intensify Tane’s negative appraisals or beliefs.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s negative appraisals cause ordinary situations or cues to become triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that the traumatic memory itself makes cues or situations become triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s sense of threat directly brings on the trauma memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s avoidance or other maladaptive strategies increase or create triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not clearly state in one paragraph that Tane’s maladaptive coping directly heightens his sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

If he caught himself relaxing at home after dinner, or felt unexpectedly happy during a quiet evening, he would tense almost immediately, as if calm were the moment danger slipped in unnoticed.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Those moments did not just unsettle him; they seemed to prove something to him about the world, that safety was a trick and that he was still the kind of man who could be blindsided without warning.
<<<END>>>

<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Once he saw life that way, ordinary situations he would once have dismissed—a quiet corridor, a delayed response, a dim hallway—began to snag on his attention and take on the charge of warning signs.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The same moments could bring back the disaster with disturbing sensory force. In the dark, or when he entered certain locations, he could suddenly smell the rank mix of floodwater and fuel again and taste the foul metallicness that had filled his mouth that night; at times the memory was so extreme it felt unreal, as if he were describing something that had happened to someone else.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Afterward, those sensations seemed to spread the storm into more of his life, so that darkness, stale air, and unfamiliar buildings no longer felt like neutral details but like cues he had to treat as dangerous.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
That belief made him scan harder in silence and grow more alarmed by delays, because any pause seemed like proof that disaster was already unfolding somewhere out of sight. It also colored the way he remembered the hurricane: the sensory fragments arrived with more force when he was caught in that helpless frame of mind, and the very extremity of the memory reinforced his feeling that normal rules did not apply and safety could not be trusted.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
On days when he was most braced for something to go wrong, the memory came faster and harder, as if the sense of danger itself were pulling the hotel night back into the room with him.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The more he avoided relaxing and kept to known places, the more foreign and dangerous unfamiliar settings became.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
His efforts to stay safe had gradually marked whole categories of places and states of mind as risky, until even the route around a stairwell or the decision not to linger in a quiet building made those things feel loaded before he had even entered them.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time his ways of coping deepened the problem. He smoked more heavily during the workday, especially before entering unfamiliar office buildings, and structured his schedule to avoid lingering anywhere that might let him relax.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because he kept leaving, bracing, and dosing himself with cigarettes instead of finding out a place was tolerable, his body never seemed to learn anything new; the danger continued to feel immediate, as if all that vigilance were still necessary.
<<<END>>>
